speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 121) respecting the Globe Printing Company.- Mr. Clarke (Essex).
Seeing this is in connection with the Toronto ' Globe,' I think we should have some explanation of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The ' Globe ' is generally able to explain itself. This Bill relates to matters of internal economy-not political^ economy-in the management of the business of this company. The Bill affects only the shareholders who are thoroughly protected.
On subsection 3 of section 3: Increase of capital stock.

It has always occurred to me that there is something defective in the manner of allotting stock. This provides that the directors may make by-laws to allot stock, and it has this redeeming feature that these by-laws must be confirmed by the shareholders. I think the Bill ought to go further and provide that wThen stock is to be allotted it should be allotted according to the present holdings. There is nothing in this or in any of these Acts to prevent the directors allotting that stock to any one they choose although, the stock may be worth much more than par. The only time at which the shareholders could discuss the allotment of stock would be when they wrere asked to confirm the by-law, and I do not know if a discussion at that time would be effective.
I think subsection 3 of section 2 covers that.
It is only in the event of default being made as to the manner of allotting stock in the by-law.
If subsection 3 is not acted upon in the mode prescribed the directors may do as they please.
The by-law has to receive the consent of two-thirds of the number of shareholders.

A by-law is submitted for the approval of the shareholders. Once the by-law is approved the shareholders have no control over it whatever, and the directors can go on and allot the stock as they see fit.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

["If this resolution compels the government to proceed with the expenditure of money forthwith there are rules applicable to it, first, that contained in the British North America Act and, second, a rule of our own House. Section 54 of the British North America Act, which has already been referred to, would prevent the adoption of such a resolution. Rule 77 of our own rules would also prevent the adoption of the resolution if it were not recommended by the Governor General and preceded by consideration in the Committee of the Whole. There are precedents mentioned by Sir John Bourinot of certain resolutions that have been adopted, but Bourinot also states that they were generally evasions of the rule. I may be allowed to read a few lines from it:
A practice lias grown up in the House of allowing the introduction of resolutions by private members, when they do not directly involve the expenditure of public money, hut simply express au abstract opinion on a matter which may necessitate a future grant. As this is a question not always understood, it may be explained that such resolutions, being framed in general terms, do not bind the House to future legislation on the subject, and are merely intended to point out to the government the importance and necessity of such expenditure.
Referring to this right of members to move such abstract resolutions, all authorities agree that it is one 'which the House exercises, and should always exercise with great reserve, and only under peculiar and exceptional circumstances.' Such resolutions are considered virtually 'an evasion of the rules of the House, and are on that account objectionable, and should be discouraged as much as possible.' Nevertheless, neither the English nor Canadian House of Commons has ever agreed to the adoption of a rule to fetter their discretion in regard to the entertaining of such propositions.
I see by the Standing Rules and Orders of the British House that- rule 71, which was passed on the 20th March, 1866, previous to confederation, reads as follows:

If any motion be made in tbe House for any aid, grant or charge upon the public revenue, whether payable out of the consolidated fund or out of money to be provided by parliament, or for any charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof shall not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the House shall think fit to appoint, and then it shall be referred to a Committee of the Whole House before any resolution or vote of the House do pass therein.
The only point I have to decide is whether the adoption of this amendment would compel the government of the day to proceed forthwith with this expenditure. I think it would, and therefore it is in violation of the rule that requires previous recommendations of the Crown and consideration by the Committee of the Whole House. Therefore, I declare the amendment out of order."]

Of all the things that have been said in reference to the agreement, probably more than one half of them con.cern that question of traffic, and
I,	therefore, think it important to call the-attention of the House and the country to-that special feature of the question. Possibly the principal mover in the matter at Washington, at least-and it has even been alleged that he is one of the principal movers in the matter within the limits of our own country-has been Mr. J.	J. Hill, who commands a very large influence in the transportation of the neighbouring republic, as -well as some influence in Canada. The question of transportation assumed considerable intensity after the present government came into power. I date the practical question of the construction of the Georgian Bay canal from the year 1903, when, after this government had been in power some seven years, it was decided to refer the whole question of transportation
to a commission. That commission was composed in the first instance oi Sir Wm. Van Horne, Mr. Bertram, who sat in this House, and Mr. Kennedy, oi Winnipeg. Sir Wm. Van Horne did not accept, so I do not quote him as an authority in this relation; Mr. Bertram was lost to us while he was proceeding with the study of the question; and ultimately the bulk of the work fell upon Mr. Reford, as chairman* Mr. Frye, and Mr. Ashdown, of Winnipeg. The object of that commission to study the question in all its phases, and make a full report to the government. They did so* and in 1905, two years after their nomination, they presented to the government a full report. It has often been conceded in this House that no commission upon a subject of importance has cost the country SO' little or has been so painstaking in its work or has presented conclusions with, which so little fault has been found. I have on more than one occasion since that commission presented its report called the attention of the government to it in connection with the execution of public works* and on each of those occasions the government has declared that it accepted that report in its entirety, that.it has not been shelved, as I sometimes hinted that it had been, but that the government was carrying out its conclusions and intended carrying them out to a finality. Now, let me quote to you the words of that report upon the point which I am now endeavouring to bring to the notice of the House, in the hope that we may have from the government an authoritative statement as to what its present intentions are. At page 21 of the report, it says:
Your Commission unhesitatingly affirm their belief in the desirability of a through waterway from the head of Lake Superior to ocean navigation, to aid in the carriage of the grain and the regulation of rates of a standard not less than that above set forth, so that the largest vessels navigating the Great Lakes can continue their voyage to ocean navigation or as near thereto as possible. But in view of the fact that the government has undertaken the survey of a proposed route by way of the French river to Lake Nipissing and thence by way of the Ottawa river to Montreal, and as the feasibility of this route from a commercial as well as an engineering point of view, and if feasible, its cost has not yet been ascertained, and further in view of the fact that the government has also undertaken the survey of the Welland canal and its vicinity, looking to its possible enlargement and diversion, your Commission do not see their way clear to any recommendation as to route, but would recommend that, in the case of the Ottawa river scheme because, of want of feasibility from a commercial or engineering point of view, or on account of its cost or for other reason, be not adopted, then the Welland canal be enlarged and deepened to the standard of the Sault Ste. Marie canal, with a view of enabling vessels

[DOT]'of the largest size to continue their voyage to Kingston or Prescott, thus bringing their *cargo to within, say 180 miles or less of Montreal before discharging the same.
I quote this passage to show that subject io two conditions-ascertaining the feasibility of the route and its cost-the commissioners were unanimous in calling upon the government to construct the Georgian Bay canal as a necessary link in our transportation system and the best and cheapest. Since then Mr. Reford, the chairman of the commission, in view of transportation improvements and .nanal works going on in the United States, sent an additional report to the government in the shape of a letter, which I have not been able to find, hut which was published at the time in the press of the country, in which Mr. Beford anew urged upon the government the *necessity of immediately carrying out the work of the Georgian Bay canal. And, as to the two conditions mentioned in that *report, these have since been fulfilled in a satisfactory way. We have ascertained by the survey instituted by the government at the time the absolute feasibility of this great waterway. We also have ascertained its cost. That survey has cost us, I believe, not less than $500,000. More than that, on every occasion when it has been possible for the government to be called upon to give an answer to those who were anxious to know whether this necessary link in our .purely Canadian transportation scheme would be carried out, the government, and also the Prime Minister, I believe, on more than one occasion, have declared that the waterway must be opened to our all-Canadian traffic; in other words, that the Georgian Bay canal should be constructed. And the last time, I think, when a delegation interviewed the Prime Minister on that .point, he added that it should be constructed without delay. In the United *States newspapers, in their government reports and in reviews, which undertake to treat the question of transportation, there has been a unanimous agreement and admission that successful rivalry with the Toute of transportation opened by the Georgian Bay canal would not be possible and that if that great work was carried out, we thereby assure for all time to our country the vast trade of the whole west, not only on our side of the line but of the western states as well. If one takes the trouble to examine the distances, there can be no doubt that a strong presumption is created at once that that admission has not been *made without cause on both sides of the line. Let me give the House, briefly, the figures:

You have there the Georgian Bay canal route by water direct, 300 miles shorter than any other Canadian route, and 432 miles shorter than any American route. And there is no transhipment, whereby half the cost is saved, for you can take a cargo by steamer carrying 12,000 tons, without breaking bulk, right through from the the grain gathering ports of the west to the sea-board. In addition to this, you have features of this route which have often been adverted to and are well known. You have the advantage of opening up a country known to us as one of vast resources-a new country1; bringing freights through without breaking bulk, you have the assurance of return freight, and yon develop great manufacturing power. The result of the very complete survey made by the government engineers is to show that, as soon as this great waterway is established, we should have over 1,000,000 horse-power. In the immediate vicinity of the great manufacturing centre of Montreal is power to the extent of over 70,000 horse-power, ready to be used. In fact, the opinion has often been expressed, and is undoubtedly well founded, that when that immense waterpower development which will be made possible by the construction of this waterway is completed, the government can assure itself of sufficient revenue from the leasing of water-powers to pay the interest upon the cost of the canal, which cost has been calculated at about $100,000,000.
I need not do more than point out to the House the immense advantage we_ should enjoy in having this route exclusively to ourselves, without any interference from our neighbours. Not only is it economically the best and shortest, but it is a route exclusively upon our own territory. There is no danger of any diversion of traffic upon that route to our neighbours. The House must be aware that our neighbours can go through our canals to Lake Ontario as freely as we do; and once traffic from the west has reached Lake Ontario, it is not impossible to carry it to the waters of the Hudson. That question has been studied. Some engineers have difficulties in the way;

Members of the House have seen within the past few days that the question has been -mooted of a common waterway with our neighbours over the St. Lawrence route. I do not know if my right hon. friend has the same pious disposition in regard to waterways, but it seems to me that we are well founded in hoping that we have not waited too long when we have within our reach all that is necessary in order to warrant us in beginning the construction of this great waterway. In seconding the motion presented by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monkl, I deiire to make a few remarks. I heartily concur in the remarks he has made, and in the resolution he has placed in your hands. On several previous occasions I have spoken at some length upon this question, and have endeavoured to urge upon the government the desirability of commencing the construction of_ this great work. I believe that the time is at hand when the Georgian Bay canal will need to be constructed, and the work should very soon be commenced, and pushed forward to completion with the least possible delay. It has been stated that the work of construction will occupy a period of about ten years. If that be the case every moment's delay means a check in the progress of Canada, especially in so far as our transportion requirements are concerned. It is not necessary for me to dwell at length upon the immense advantages which would accrue to this country by the improvement of this waterway. It is a national project, and will tend to ensure the carriage of our products through an all-Canadian route. It will cement the east and the west by an exchange of products. Our Nova Scotian coal will find a market in northern and western Ontario, and the grain and wheat of the Northwest will be transported to the east. It will effect a saving in the cost of transportation of from two to four cents to the farmers of the west on every bushel of grain which they produce. It will promote the development of our water-powers to the extent of more than a million horse-power, and in so doing will tend to build up industries throughout the country. It-will bring Fort William, Sault Ste. Marie and Duluth 282 miles nearer to Montreal than they are by the St. Lawrence route. In short, Mr. Speaker, it will afford the quickest and most direct route from the great lakes to the seaboard. There are a great many other advantages which I

could mention, but I do not wish to delay the House more than to bring to your attention one of the resolutions which was adopted recently by the city council of Montreal:
Montreal, Nov. 28.-At a meeting of the city council this afternoon Aid. Lapointe submitted a resolution in favour of the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. The motion which was adopted without discussion and will be forwarded to Ottawa, was as follows :-
Whereas the construction of the Georgian Bay canal would afford for the produce of the northern and western parts of the American continent the shortest and most advantageous route, and would add an incalculable element of progress and prosperity to the commerce, agriculture and industry of Canada, and thereby to the city of Montreal, would accrue immense advantage, be it resolved that the parliament of Canada be requested to carry out this essentially national enterprise with the shortest possible delay.
Within the last month I understand that a petition was presented to this government signed by 60,000 influential men in the city of Montreal urging upon the government the necessity of building this great waterway. In so far as the improvement and betterment of other waterways throughout this country is concerned, I do not wish to place myself on record as being opposed to the improvement of any waterway that is' going to be in the interest of the 'transportation requirements of the country. I believe, as my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has said, that this country will require the Hudson Bay railway, the deepening of the Welland canal and the building of the Georgian Bay canal, but the Georgian Bay canal project has been before the country for a great many years, it has been proved conclusively that it is a feasible proposition, that it will shorten the distance between the Great Lakes and the sea-board by from 200 to 300 miles, and in view of the fact that it is going to be a great benefit to the country, not only from the transportation standpoint, but from the development which will take place by the improvement of the water-powers along the route, I believe it is time that the government took action and commenced the construction of this great work. Let us commence its construction to-day, to-morrow may be too late, and let us see to it that Canadian products are transported through Canadian channels to the markets of the world, and in this way bind together the component parts of this great country of ours.

Mr Speaker, the subject before the House has Such a wide scope that I feel that it will require more time, and a better occasion to speak upon it than the one which has been
offered to us to-day by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I have so often spoken on this subject of the very early construction of the Georgian Bay canal, that I feel it is somewhat superfluous to put myself again upon record as an adherent of the project. I believe, without any vain boasting, that this House will agree with me that I am as strongly in favour of the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, which has been proven by my words in this House, as is the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. It is so seldom that I am able to agree with that hon. gentleman that I am particularly pleased this afternoon to he able to congratulate him upon his speech although I am not able to congratulate him upon the propriety of the manner in which he has brought before the House this discussion upon the question of the Georgian Bay canal. On Friday last my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), when making his very able statement in this House, referred in a few words to the policy that it is understood this government would follow in a short time in connection with the Georgian Bay canal. The House will pardon me if I refer to his words which are to be found in ' Hansard ' of March 10, page 5161. In referring to the canal system I had incidentally made the remark that I believed the Georgian Bay canal route was the proper route between the Great Lakes and the sea-ports and my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals said in connection with that:
My hon. friend behind me has said that the Georgian Bay canal route is the route. I would discuss the question of the Georgian Bay canal route at greater length but for the fact that it is not in my department, and I am supposed to be discussing questions connected with my department. I might say distinctly that I believe it is in the interest of Canada from one end to the other to enter upon both enterprises and at a not very far distant date. We must remember that When we bring the products of the great west to the east the products of the east are carried back to the west, and if we could take the time to go into the prospects for increasing that trade in a few years, we would arrive at a conclusion that it is necessary-in the interest of the Canadian carrying trade?-no, it is necessary in the interest of the people who produce in Canada, as well as who buy goods in Canada, that these two great waterways should be developed by the people of Canada, and I believe that no greater interest would accrue from any investment that the people could make than that which would result from the development of these two waterways. My hon. friend will see that I am quite clear upon this subject, and that the diffidence I have about discussing it in detail only arises from the fact that it is not in my department, but I believe in these projects just the same.

So we have the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux), a few days ago, speaking in the city of Montreal, in a very able speech, also declared that he was strongly in favour of the early construction of the Georgian Bay canal. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) has put himself upon record in the same sense. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) likewise, and when we come to the last and certainly not the least member of the Canadian cabinet we have the.right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who has said, in the city of Hull, and I believe in other parts of this country, that h'e was strongly of the belief that the Georgian Bay canal should be constructed at as early a date as possible. That ought to be satisfactory to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, and to the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. White). But apparently these hon. gentlemen, seeing a question of vital import before this House, and before the country at the present moment-I refer to the question of reciprocity with the United States and seeing that the country is entirely in favour of reciprocity and that the great majority of this House are in favour of reciprocity, they want to put if possible an obstacle in the way of the carrying out of this agreement by bringing up the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. If, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) had brought the matter before the House in a sensible way -well, perhaps it is not parliamentary to say that-but, had he brought it before the House in a judicious way, then I am sure he would have every hon. member on this side of the House supporting him. But, bringing it up as a vote of want of confidence in the government, he knows perfectly well that the members of this side of the House who have confidence in the government and wish to see the Georgian Bay canal built are not going to vote against the government so as to kill the project in its infancy. That would not be sane, that would not be judicious, and yet that is what the hon. member (Mr. Monk) asks us to do. Now, I begin to doubt that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier iMr. Monk) is truly in favour of the Georgian Bay canal, and his action in bringing forward this motion to-day gives me cause to doubt. I shall give my reasons for that doubt-the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) believes in the construction of the Georgian Bay canal and he has submitted to the House on more than one occasion a resolution favouring it, and wishing to assure himself of the support of hon. members of this House he has had the common courtesy to notify hon. gentlemen Mr. DEVLIN.
who are in favour of the canal that he would propose his motion at a certain time.

It has become so current with gentlemen on the other side of the House, that now when they attack anybody on this side they automatically refer to the hon. member for North Toronto. I do not think the hon. member for Ottawa really means to refer to me; I do not want all the honours.

Now, the hon. member (Mr. Monk) knows perfectly well that the question of reciprocity is not going to affect adversely the Georgian Bay canal. He knows perfectly well that an agreement of reciprocity with the United States will add to the necessity for the Georgian Bay canal. He knows perfectly well that the farmers of this country are clamouring for two things: Reciprocity and the Georgian Bay canal, and he knows that if you add to the wealth of the farmers of this country and to the possibilities of the increased production of grain you will of necessity require increased transportation facilities, and you will have to look for that to an improved waterways system. I have here the report of the Trade and Commerce Department, and I am fairly amazed to see from it the quantity of grain that has been coming from Port Arthur and Fort William by the water route. I find that our exports from Canada to the United States during the year 1907-and I refer now solely to Canadian produce-amounted to $92,283,500 worth, while in 1910 they reached $106,153,900 worth, from which it appears that

Canada's trade with the United States is constantly increasing.
Have you the figures showing the trade the United States did with Canada?

Yes. The dutiable imports into Canada from the United States in 1907 amounted to $116,159,883 and the dutiable imports into Canada from the United States in 1910 amounted to the amazing sum of $143,777,541, which, of course goes to prove my statement, that the trade between the two countries is increasing. 1 am not a believer in the doctrine which is often preached in this House by the hon. member for North Toronto, that an increase in imports means an impoverished country; on the contrary I believe that increasing imports indicates that a country is wealthy. I therefore say that the trade between Canada and the United States is constantly on the increase, and the grain production of Canada also being constantly on the increase, as a consequence we require increased transportation facilities I find in the Trade and Navigation Returns a statement showing the receipts and shipments of grain at Fort William and Port Arthur from September 1st to January 31st. and in the month of September 1910 there were shipped from Fort William and Port Arthur by rail 241,362 bushels, and in the same month by lake 4,042,958 bushels of wheat alone.
There was a similar quantity of oats less of barley and less of flax. In the month of September there were 327,599 bushels bv rail and 5,256,055 bushels by lake; in the month of October there were 455,709 bushels by rail and 17,765.528 bushels by lake; in the month of November there were 958 915 by rail and 21,279,964 bushels by lake Now where is this grain going to? It is going to the United Kingdom and to the United [states. The greater quantity is going to the United Kingdom, and the United Kingdom will continue to take a great quantity of our grain-there is no gainsaying that. Any hon. gentleman has simply to refer to the British parliamentry debates to see that Canada will continue through all time to supply, not alone the United Kingdom, but the world, with grain. The production of Canada is constantly on the increase while the production of the United States is consequently on the decrease. Canada's area of grain-producing is a wonderful area. The wheat belt of western Canada is four times the size of the wheat belt of the whole United States; so that hon. gentlemen opposite need not have any fear that our grain production will not constantly be on the increase. That being so, I ask you if it will not be necessary for us to build the Georgian Bay canal? And reciprocity with the United otates will only enhance, and will not depreciate, as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier would lead us to believe, the value of the Georgian Bay canal. We have a great many members of the cabinet of this country on record as being in favour of the construction of that great work; we have a great many members of this House committed to its construction; we have the press of a great section of this country, as well as many boards of trade, clamouring for it. The Georgian Bay canal is one of my pet subjects, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to go on speaking on it all afternoon and all evening; but I know that there are a number of other hon. members of this House who are only too anxious to give utterance to their views upon this 'subject. I see the Postmaster General, (Mr. Lemieux), for instance-lie hardly ever misses an opportunity to proclaim what a strong believer he is in the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. The hen. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), who is very familar with the waterways of this country is also a strong believer in it. I know that these hon. gentlemen will give expression to their views on this subject. But I would like to point out another reason not commonly given for the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. We shall require it for the carrying of our minerals; and, as a great portion of the canal will pass through the province of Quebec, let me point out that that province, as a producer of minerals, is getting richer every year. I know that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier will attribute that directly to the fact that in the province of Quebec there is good, government. Whatever may be the cause, the mineral wealth of the province of Quebec is constantly increasing. In 1909 the value of the mineral production of Quebec amounted to $5,552,062, and in 1910 it amounted to $7,072,244. That included asbestos, iron, cement and other minerals which will be shipped by water. Therefore, if we wish to carry our mineral production to a successful issue, we must construct the Georgian Bay canal.
Now, Sir, I am not going to support the motion of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, because the hon. member has brought it in for a political purpose. If not, why did he allow so many years to go by without placing a resolution on the Order Paper in favour of the Georgian Bay canal? Why did he bring it in this particular way, just at a moment when he knew that it involved a vote of want of confidence in the government? Does he imagine for a moment that the country, especially that portion which is interested in the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, is so innocent as to believe that a vote for his amendment will mean the immediate construction of the canal? Before I cast a vote upon this amendment, which would mean, if carried, the defeat

515&
of the government, I would like to ask the hon. leader of the opposition if, following out the wording of the amendment, he were called upon to form a government, would he immediately begin the construction of the Georgian Bay canal?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the hon. gentlemen is asking me for some instruction as to how he should vote, I would like to say before I answer that I would require some guarantee that he would follow the advice.

The leader of the opposition is a ishrewd lawyer, and I know that he does not want to commit himself, and it would be hardly fair for me to try to exact a committal from him. I take it that the opposition have not made up their minds what their policy would be with regard to the construction of the Georgian Bay canal if they came into power, which thank Heaven will not be for many a day; and, therefore, it would ill become me to help to defeat the present government and help to bring the opposition into power in order to delay the construction of that great work. Earnestly believing in the early construction of the Georgian Bay canal, I do not think that I could logically vote with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. I appreciate his kindly sentiments towards this project and also toward hon. members of this House who favour the early carrying of this project to a successful issue. But Sir, as I have had occasion to say before in this House, timeo Danaos et dona ferentes-I fear the Greeks even when bringing gifts-and I fear the hon. member for Jacques Cartier because of his manner of bringing this subject before the House. I trust that every hon. member on this side at least, who is in favour of the early construction of the' Georgian Bay canal will see that we have one hope for the realization of our wishes, and that is to pin our faith to the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who is earnest in his belief that this work should proceed, and who will proceed with it. His life has been given to great works, such as the construction of the Transcontinental road, and the reform which is to bring wealth to the farmers of Canada, improved trade relations with the United States, and who, I believe, as the crowning work of his life, will undertake the early-carrying out of the construction of the Georgian Bay canal.

I have no desire to follow the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) in his varied wanderings. Nor have I any desire to oast reflections upon those who are in favour of the early complete deepening of the Welland canal or the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. I believe that all these works will be necessary in a few years to solve the transportation problem of Can-Mr. DEVLIN.
ada. We heard the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) state on Friday last, that the canal traffic of Canada had incresed from 5,665,259 tons in 1901 to 42,990,608 tons in 1910-an increase in nine years of 660 per cent. According to the reports of the engineers, ten years will be required for the construction of this contemplated Georgian Bay canal. If we increase one-fourth or even one-tenth as fast as in the last ten years, there will be traffic awaiting this canal by the time it is finished. The Georgian Bay canal is in a somewhat different position from any other great work now in contemplation in Canada, including the great works that I have indicated. We have a complete survey of this canal,-and not only one, but many surveys. We have one completed, I think, in 1907, which cost the Dominion of Canada upwards of $1,000,000, a survey in every way complete; and I have yet to hear that any attempt has yet been made to refute any of the statements made in the report of the engineers. In this report, the engineers were unanimous. They agreed in the opinion that this canal would be a great project, valuable to the country, and entirely feasible in every way. The hon. member for Wright has taken occasion to call the attention of the House to the fact that a great many of the ministers of the Crown, have, on various occasions, spoken in favour of this project. I myself, have heard several of them make remarks of that nature. But these were made years ago. They had the facts then that they have now; and I support the motion of the hon. member foT Jacques Cartier, simply for the same reason that I would support a similar motion if it were made by the hon. member for Wright. Those of us who are in favour of the early completion of this canal-and I think that in this we speak for the majority of the people of Canada-should support any action that will conduce to the carrying into effect of our wishes.
There is another subject mentioned by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, which demands a good deal of attention, and that is the question of cost. It must be evident to everybody that, if the land in Montreal and its vicinity that will be necessary for the construction of this canal were expropriated at this time, it would mean a great saving in the ultimate cost of the canal. There is also the fact that the government has been spending large sums of money for the conservation and regulation of the water flow on the Ottawa river. These works could go hand in hand, with the works for the canal. We had on Lake Nipissing dams put in under the direction of the Minister of Public Works for the control of the waters of the lake. But these were found un-

successful, and the country was put to the cost of blowing them out with dynamite. I understand that they are being built a second time under the Department of Public Works. All this work would be unnecessary, for the control of the water in these lakes and rivers would be effected by the works in the construction of the canal. There is also the matter of water-powers. *Canada has just awakened to the value of the water-powers of Ontarioiland of Quebec and of the Dominion as a whole. The Minister of Railways on Friday last stated that the expenditure upon the Trent canal, .great as it was, and little commercial value as it will have when completed, was entirely justified by the great water-powers that had been developed along that route. Contrast the water-powers of the Trent canal with those along the Georgian Bay canal, whether you consider them from the point of view of accessibility, volume or in any other way.
I have no desire to take up the time of the House further. This matter has been thoroughly gone into on other occasions; and I do not think it necessary that I should place myself further on record in the matter. In conclusion, I might say a word in answer to the hon. member for Wright, when he claims that he is called upon to vote against this motion because it is a vote of want of confidence. A few days ago, the hon member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. .Monk) brought in an amendment to an exactly similar motion, which amendment was accepted by the government and for which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Devlin) voted. I have no hesitation in saying that the government has the same option to-day as it had at that time; if they choose, they can accept the amendment of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier and agree to its unanimous adoption by this House.

speakeroldname: Hon. WILLIAM PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Intensely interested as I am in the early construction of this most Important link in the chain of Canadian transportation, I feel the deepest possible regret that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has introduced his motion at the present time and in the form in which he has introduced it. Heretofore,- and I speak now of what is within my knowledge of the course of events so far as this great work is concerned, extending over a great many years-never until today has the subject taken on a party aspect. Years ago, when the Montreal, Ottawa & Georgian Bay Canal Company first presented its project to parliament, I happened to be one of the counsel employed by the company. I knew what efforts the company bad made to bring the matter before the attention of parliament and the
public, and it was a matter of gratification to me, as well as to those for whom I was acting at the time, that hon. members of this House dealt with the question from a broad standpoint, entirely irrespective of party. I remember that, on o-ne occasion, upwards of a hundred members on both sides of the House, irrespective of whether they were Liberals or Conservatives, signed a memorial in favour of the construction of this canal. At the last session of parliament, and also, I think, at the session before, motions were made for peturns on this subject, and different members spoke in support of the project. I am sure that hon. members who Tecall those discussions will agree with me that these motions were supported by hon. members of this House irrespective of their party affiliations, and that on each of these occasions the project was spoken of with warm sympathy by the Tight hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and by other members of the House.
But to-day the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has chosen, for what purpose I know not, for he certainly does not seem to be acting the part of a friend of this great project, to throw into it an element of partisanship. The very resolution he has moved introduces a matter in regard to which we cannot all agree. The hon. gentleman, instead of urging that the government should seriously consider the early construction of this canal, asks that the House shall, in effect, instruct the government to immediately begin its construction, and why? Because of the possible diversion of traffic to the country to the south. The hon. gentleman knows very well that a majority of the members in this House do not share that view. The hon. gentleman knows that nothing has recently occurred and nothing is likely to occur in the near future which would be likely to divert Canadian traffic to the country to the south of us. This canal, when it is constructed, is intended primarily to carry the products of the west to the ports upon the St, Lawrence for shipment to the markets of the old world; any products of the west which may be required by our neighbours to the south and which may be purchased for home consumption would not pass through this canal for the reason I have stated. If I were framing a resolution in order to bring this matter properly before the House, instead of putting it as my hon. friend has, that there might be a diversion of our products to the country to the south I would rather have said:	In view of the anticipated continuation of the rapid development of the Canadian west, and the .unrivalled position that the city of Montreal

and other St. Lawrence ports will, when the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay canal is constructed, occupy for the export of the products not only of the Canadian west, but of a large portion of the country to the south of us,.in the opinion of this House it is desirable that the government should consider seriously the early construction of this canal. If my hon. friend had moved a substantive motion ol that character, I have no doubt it would have met with a sympathetic response from both sides of the House. I am sure it would have met with a sympathetic reception on the part of the government and I believe also on the part of all the supporters of the government. I say that because upon the occasion when a very large delegation last met the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues and ^.presented in the very strongest way possible, the importance of engaging upon the early con-structiion of this canal, my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) told that delegation that it was not necessary to come to the government with arguments in support of this great project. He told ..them that he and his colleagues were thoroughly impressed with the necessity of undertaking the construction of the canal at the earliest possible moment, but that it was simply a question of finances, that whenever the Finance Minister, in the exercise of his judgment, informed his colleagues ..that the time had arrived when the government could safely ask parliament to give it authority to begin the construction of this important work, then at that moment, and the Prime Minister expressed the hope that that moment would soon arrive, the government would be prepared to submit to parliament a project for the .construction of the canal. I would ask my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier in view of what has been said by the Prime Minister, in view of the expressions of -opinion which have been given in this House by prominent members of both sides in the past, and if he seriously desires to see the early construction of this canal, whether it is desirable that he should at this time introduce into the _ discussion of this great question, something of partisanship and submit a resolution, in regard to certain parts of which it would be impossible for all the members of this House to agree. I commend the matter to my hon. friend, because as I have said, J am sincerely in favour of the construction of this most important work.
I recognize the enormous benefit it would be to the transportation interests of Canada. I recognize that when this canal is built, it is going to command the traffic, not only of the Canadian west, but much Mr. PUGSLEY.
of the trade of the States which lie to the south of the boundary line. -If my hon. friend had been here on Friday last, I am sure he would have been greatly interested in the most admirable speech made by the hon, member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) who has always been a friend of the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay canal. In that speech the hon. gentleman dwelt in the strongest possible terms upon the great importance of this work. He showed how important it would be to Canada, important not only to .western Canada, but to eastern Canada as well. He spoke as a friend, as one who for years has been in earnest sympathy with this work, and he did not seek to throw into the discussion of the question with regard to its construction any element such as that which the hon. member for Jacques Cartier has sought to throw into the.^dis-cussion to-day.
With regard to my own department and to the attitude of the government towards this work, it ought not to be necessary to do anything further than draw attention to the fact that a number of years ago the government decided to ask this parliament for authority to proceed with a most exhaustive survey of the route of that canal. Years have been spent upon that work. A board of engineers was organized and the work was placed under the control of some of the most experienced and capable engineers of the department. I do not hesitate to say that they have done their work in the most thorough and conscientious manner; I do not hesitate to say, and I appeal to the judgment of members who have seen the report that the report they have made and the plans they have submitted, the detailed plans prepared which are now before parliament, show that they have done their work in the most exhaustive and satisfactory manner. Their reports show that the construction of the canal is not only feasible, but that it can be carried out at a cost which no one will say would, now or in the near future, be beyond the financial resources of the people of Canada. The cost is placed at something like $100,000,; 000. That, bear in mind, is not merely for a 14 foot canal as at first proposed, but for a canal having a depth of 22 feet, over the mitre sills, a canal which will enable quite large ocean steamers to pass right through to Lake Huron and on to the ports on the western shores of our great inland lakes. That canal will be quite capable of giving accommodation to ocean traffic. The jrro-ject has assumed proportions far beyond what was thought of in the early days when the fondest hopes of the people of this country Ionly looked forward to >a canal with a depth of some 14 feet

The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) refers to what the United States has done in the way of building canals, and says that Canada has done little. I entirely disagree in that respect. The Erie canal, to which he has referred, is but little more than a great ditch, having a depth of only 9 feet, whereas our system of canals, extending from Lake St. Clair down to the city of Montreal, has a uniform depth of not less than 14 feet, thus giving accommodation to very much larger boats which are capable of carrying a very much larger tonnage than can be accommodated by the Erie canal. I think there as no reflection to be made on the people of Canada so far as their enterprise in the past in regard to the construction of our great system of canals has been concerned, and I think the very fact that the government had surveys made, shows that we are favourably considering the construction of a great canal which will have a depth not of 9 feet as the Erie canal, not of 14 feet as the St. Lawrence, at the present moment, but a depth _pf 22 feet capable of accommodating large ocean vessels and enabling them to proceed right up t<\ Port Arthur and Fort William.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, let me say again that I regret exceedingly that my hon. friend has introduced this resolution in the way he has chosen. I regret its terms, and it does seem to me that my hon. friend, upon reflection, knowing what has been the expressed feelings of members of the House in regard to this project in the past, whenever it has been brought to the attention of the House in a non-partisan way, will feel that in thus presenting his motion he is not acting as a friend of this scheme, but he is acting in a way which is rather calculated to retard the undertaking.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I desire to call your attention to the fact that in my judgment the motion of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) is out of order. By the rules of the House, and by the amended rules of the House also, no private member can make a motion which involves an appropriation of public money or a charge upon the revenue. According to the principles of parliamentary government, the responsibility for all public expenditures rests altogether upon the Crown and its advisers; it is not within the province of any member of parliament to make a motion which involves an expenditure of money by parliament. The principle is so well recognized that it is not necessary to refer to it. Still, I will call your attention to rule 53, which enacts:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address, or Bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any
tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address, or Bill is proposed.
This enactment is not new, it is simply a reproduction of a rule which is as old as parliamentary government in England. But the framers of the British North America Act attached so much importance to this rule that they did not leave it to be ordinarily applied as a rule of the House, as it existed in 1867, but they put it in the . constitution in still more positive language. Now, the motion of my hon. friend reads as follows:
The House, in view of a possible diversion of the country's carrying trade from Canadian channels, and in order to ensure the most favourable conditions of transportation between western points and the Canadian Atlantic seaboard, records its opinion and determination that the construction of the Georgian Bay canal should be commenced forthwith

Now nothing could be more positive than these terms, the House is asked to express a determination that without a moment's delay the construction of the canal should be commenced. Now, everybody is aware that it is allowable to a member of the House, not to propose a direct motion such as this, calling for an expenditure of money, but a motion which invites the attention of the government or of the House to the advisability of providing for an expenditure of some kind. In this respect the rights of members of the House are well defined, but they are limited. While a member may, by a motion, express a desire or declare a policy in abstract terms, the moment the motion goes beyond abstract terms, and the moment he goes so far as to enjoin upon the government the immediate duty of providing for an expenditure, then he overrides the rule. Let me call the attention of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier to the last edition of May, 1906, page 571, where he will find the following words apply directly to his motion:
To a certain extent, evasions are, by usage, permitted of the restriction imposed by the standing orders upon proposals for the expenditure of public money. Bills devising a large scheme for public expenditure, accompanied by provisions for the application of the same, have been brought in upon motion, the money clauses being printed in italics. In such cases, the principle of the Bill is discussed, and, if approved on behalf of the CrowTn, the necessary pecuniary provision is subsequently made; otherwise further progress of the Bill is prevented by the refusal of the Royal recommendation. In like manner, motions advocating public expenditure, or the imposition of a charge, if the motion be framed in sufficiently abstract and general terms, can be entertained, and agreed to by the House. Resolutions of this nature are

permissible because, having no operative effect, no grant is made or burden imposed by their adoption.
Now, if the motion of my hon. friend were couched in abstract terms and made general, it would be in order; but if, as I contend, his motion, far from being abstract and general, is so precise as to make an injunction upon the government at once to enter upon this expenditure, then there can be no doubt that he has gone beyond the rights assigned to a member, and has made a motion which is out of order. Now let me' ask my hon. friend to read his motion over again, and he will agree that the terms are imperative, and their effect if the House were to pass the motion, would be to put upon the government the immediate duty of proceeding with this work.
The House records its. opinion and determination that the construction of the Georgian Bay canal should be commenced forthwith.
I submit that my hon. friend has gone beyond the rights assigned to a member, and the motion is out of order, and upon this I would ask your ruling.

I think it is a great pity that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) should have gone out of his way to find in this motion a partisan spirit. If the proposed arrangements with the United States are carried into effect they will produce traffic, and if, as is contended, they will produce traffic with the United States, it is quite natural that that traffic would be removed from Canadian channels. I do not see anything in the motion that would lead anybody to believe there was a partisan motive behind the motion I have made. It calls purely and simply for a decision from the government. In answering my right hon. friend, it seems to me he has gone out of his way to avoid giving a categorical answer to the question involved in the motion. I think the public at large would have been much better pleased to see him less punctilious upon the point of order, and more anxious to give the information which is plainly sought for by this motion. We are all familiar with the rule that a private member cannot initiate public expenditure; that has been in the English constitution since 1701, I think that privilege has been with the consent of the House, reserved to the Crown. There is nothing in this motion which calls for an expenditure of money, and that is the only thing which would stop a private member from making such a motion. There is no call here for money, it is for an expression of opinion by the House, and an enjoinder, if you will, 'to the government to begin the construction of the canal.
But where do you find in that, words which correspond with the rule which my' Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
hon. friend quoted about requiring the imposition of a tax or the expenditure of any specific sum of money? That is all I have to submit on that point, Mr. Speaker. You will find authority in Bourinot for the statement that the very greatest latitude possible has been accorded since the House of Commons has existed, in the matters of motions of this kind, a motion which does not go so far as to require the spending of a specific sum of money. That is what Sir John Bourinot says in his work. There is no question of money here and it seems to me that my right hon. friend might very well have answered the question that is sought to be solved by this motion instead of taking refuge in the point of order which has no force with reference to a motion of this kind.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
If this resolution compels the government to proceed with the expenditure of money forthwith there are rules applicable to it, first, that contained in the British North America Act and, second, a rule of our own House. Section 54 of the British North America Act, which has already been referred to, would prevent the adoption of such a resolution. Rule 77 of our own rules would also prevent the adoption of the resolution if it were not recommended by the Governor General and preceded by consideration in the Committee of the Whole. There are precedents mentioned by Sir John Bourinot of certain resolutions that have been adopted, but Bourinot also states that they were generally evasions of the rule. I may be allowed to read a few lines from it:
A practice lias grown up in the House of allowing the introduction of resolutions by private members, when they do not directly involve the expenditure of public money, hut simply express au abstract opinion on a matter which may necessitate a future grant. As this is a question not always understood, it may be explained that such resolutions, being framed in general terms, do not bind the House to future legislation on the subject, and are merely intended to point out to the government the importance and necessity of such expenditure.
Referring to this right of members to move such abstract resolutions, all authorities agree that it is one 'which the House exercises, and should always exercise with great reserve, and only under peculiar and exceptional circumstances.' Such resolutions are considered virtually 'an evasion of the rules of the House, and are on that account objectionable, and should be discouraged as much as possible.' Nevertheless, neither the English nor Canadian House of Commons has ever agreed to the adoption of a rule to fetter their discretion in regard to the entertaining of such propositions.
I see by the Standing Rules and Orders of the British House that- rule 71, which was passed on the 20th March, 1866, previous to confederation, reads as follows:

If any motion be made in tbe House for any aid, grant or charge upon the public revenue, whether payable out of the consolidated fund or out of money to be provided by parliament, or for any charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof shall not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the House shall think fit to appoint, and then it shall be referred to a Committee of the Whole House before any resolution or vote of the House do pass therein.
The only point I have to decide is whether the adoption of this amendment would compel the government of the day to proceed forthwith with this expenditure. I think it would, and therefore it is in violation of the rule that requires previous recommendations of the Crown and consideration by the Committee of the Whole House. Therefore, I declare the amendment out of order.

speechtext:
We cannot be responsible for the accuracy of their figures.
