speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock, I was placing before it the figures of the immigration for the current year. I pointed out not only that the total immigration was larger than that of any previous year in the history of the country, but also, from the evidence that was at hand, that the character of the immigration was superior to that of the previous year as the character of that year's immigration was superior to that of the year preceding. I want to emphasize the fact of the larger immigration of this year, an immigration which, if our estimate of 300,000 is correct, is nearly 100,000 more than that of last year, an increase of 33J per cent, and last year's immigration was only exceeded by that of the year 1907-8. The growth of our immigration is shown by the statement that in 1897 the total immigration was 21,716, in 1900 it was 49,149, in 1905 it was 189,064, and in 1910-11 it is over 300,000. The committee will remember that some years ago the conditions surrounding the immigration into Canada were such as to call for considerable unfavourable comment. There were objections made to the character of the people who were coming:	They were not well provided with
means ; they were not sufficiently well selected as to physical and other conditions. . The immigration of the present fiscal year, although larger than that of any other fiscal year in the history of Canada, has called forth less complaint upon any of these scores than has ever before been the case in the history of immigration into Canada. That is to say, there is less lack of employment, and less of unfavourable conditions on the part of the immigrants. I will deal with what appear to me to be the reasons for this in a short time. In the meantime, I will give some information as to the means that are taken by the Immigration Department to secure this large influx of people. First, let me say that it is absolutely contrary to the policy of the Immigration Department of the Dominion government at the present time to give assistance to immigrants-to Mr. WRIGHT.
pay anything to induce an immigrant to come to Canada.
You never did.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: How does the total expenditure for immigration of last year compare with that of the preceding year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad that my hon. friend has reminded me of tnat, because while the immigration has increased from 21,000 in the year 1897 to over 300,000 in 1910, the expenditure has increased from $261,000 in 1897-98, to $960,000 in 1909-10; that is to say, that while the expenditure has increased fourfold, the returns for that expenditure have increased some fourteen fold; so that to-day the country is getting a proportionately greater value for its money than it did in 1897. I have said that Canada has no policy of assisting immigration. Canada has no money to give to any man to cause him to come to Canada; but Canada spends her money for the purpose of bringing the advantages of Canada to the attention of those who are likely to avail themselves of them. Our immigration policy is in the first instance simply an advertising policy-a means of placing the advantages of Canada before such people in other countries as we desire to induce to come to Canada in the belief that they will do well for themselves when they come here. We, therefore, keep salaried agents, advertise in newspapers, and publish literature in regard to Canada for the information of the public. Speaking in more detail, in Great Britain we nave nine salaried agents in permanent offices, whose business it is to distribute literature, to give information, to spread a knowledge of Canada wherever it can advantageously be done, and to facilitate the coming to Canada of desirable people who wish to come. On the continent of Europe we have only two such agencies, one in France and one in Belgium. In Great Britain we find that

a great deal of our publicity work is done by the booking agents, who are licensed by the British government to sell transportation. By our arrangement with these people we are enabled to get their special efforts on behalf of Canada. This is where the bonus system comes in. We pay these booking agents $5 on each ticket to Canada sold by them, provided the person buying the ticket is of the class considered desirable by us. This makes the agent interested in advertising Canada. He would rather sell tickets to Canada than to the United States or South Africa, or South America hr any other country that does not give him any extra consideration of this kind.
Is this bonus for men, women and children?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Will the minister tell us where these salaried agents in the United States are located?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the following cities: Detroit, Michigan; Spokane, Washington; Milwaukee, Wisconsin; Watertown, South Dakota; Grand Forks, North Dakota; St. Paul, Minnesota; Omaha, Nebraska; Kansas City, Missouri; Toledo, Ohio: Chicago, Illinois; Great Falls, Montana; Indianapolis, Indiana; Syracuse, New York; Boston, Massachusetts; Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, and Providence, Rhode Island.
In the United States we employ subagents who are paid an allowance based upon the number of people whom they bring in, the: allowance being at the rate of $3 for each adult male person, $2 for each woman and $1 for each child. These sub-agents are mainly useful in giving the people information as to how they ,ean best reach Canada with their effects.
The work of advertising in foreign countries and in the British islands is a large part of our immigration effort and perhaps the most important part. But another very important part is that of dealing with the immigrants after they arrive in Canada. While we do not. give any financial assistance,-that is, it is not our policy to give financial assistance, it is our policy to facilitate, as far as possible, the immigrant reaching the destination and the purpose for which he came to Canada. For that reason we have a system in the western provinces of distributing immigrants on the land. There is what might be called a central distribution office in Winnipeg in charge of the Commissioner of Immigration. All railroads of the west radiate from Winnipeg, and, at different points throughout the western provinces which

immigrants are likely to seek, we have immigration halls, that is, places where immigrants may be temporarily entertained on leaving the train and before they go out on the land. We have a number of officers known as land guides, who are paid at the rate of $2 per day and whose duty it is to guide parties out to the vacant lands. These laud guides are men who are acquainted with the run of the surveys, have some knowledge of the country, and can take a person who is not familiar with conditions in that country -and, naturally a person coming from the British islands or from continental Europe must find things very strange when he goes on the prairie-to the best land available in the neighbourhood. When the immigrant comes looking for land, arrangements may be made with the land guide, who is responsible to the government, and who will take the immigrant out and show him the land and indicate the boundaries and, generally speaking, assist in locating him. The immigrant, of course, has to pay for his own expenses, including transportation, but we give the land guide payment at the rate of $2 per day so as to retain his services.
How many of these land guides are there in the employ of the government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At this time, 65.
How are they distributed throughout the prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I co.uld not, offhand, say just where they are located, but, generally speaking, they are located so as to be in touch with the land agencies, because the land agency is the place to which the immigrant must go in order to locate his land after he has decided upon it.

Has the minister any complaints of any of these guides ' working ' these immigrants-that is, getting an extra fee for showing them the good land? The minister, I suppose, understands what I mean. There have been complaints that guides would not show land-seekers the best land unless they received $100 or $200 extra. Have any complaints of that kind been received?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have had no complaints on that line. Such complaints, if they were made to the commissioner at Winnipeg, would not likely reach me through the commissioner at Winnipeg, as I am sure that on receipt of such complaint the commissioner would dismiss the guide before the complaint reached me. If my hon. friend has any knowledge of such cases and the facts can be substantiated, I will guarantee that the guide complained of will be dismissed without delay.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In Ontario and Quebec, where the demand is not for free land, but for farm labourers, we have 125 distribution agents in the farming counties, whose business it is to see that immigrants for Ontario are distributed amongst the farmers who desire help. In 1909, we distributed 3,610 farm labourers amongst the farmers of these two provinces, and in 1910, 6,769. Thus the number of labourers supplied to farmers in this way doubled in one year. In Prince Edward Island we have had a Mr. Winfield employed for about two years. The conditions there are different again from those in Ontario and Quebec and the west. There is no great demand for farm labourers and no free land, but there is land which can be purchased at a reasonable price, so that Mr. Winfield's efforts are directed to bringing out a class of practical farmers who wish to buy land at reasonable rates. He sails on the 14th of next month with a party of this kind.	. .	,
On behalf of New Brunswick, we have had since Christmas, Mr. Craigie, of fet. John, N.B., in the old country. We have so far had no returns from him. At the moment we have no person from Nova Scotia, but expect to have before long.

Is Mr. Craigie working in connection with the local government? The local authorities have cognizance of farms in New Brunswick which can be obtained by immigrants. Would he have a list of these farms?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would think it would be part of his business to inform him in regard to the conditions there. Undoubtedly he would be informed and would take the action my hon. friend suggests. He will work in harmony with the provincial government in securing immigrants who will be likely to occupy land in New Brunswick.
Has not the government an agent in Winnipeg who receives $25 from the farmers to bring out labourers to 'Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have two agents in Manitoba for the placing of labourers and we Lave sent farm delegates from Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta during the winter to advertise and bring to the notice of the people of England, Scotland and Ireland the opportunities offered by the three provinces in the way of free land, land for purchase and employment for labourers.

I did not mean that, but before Mr. Smith was sent to London he used to send agents round to the different towns, and the farmers used to give him $25 on condition that he would supply them with the men. Whether that custom is still continued I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not being done at the present time, unless under very exceptional circumstances; I think it was not found to work out satisfactorily. I think there was a man named Adamson who did that sort of work, and while Mr. Adamson was a very good man, and brought out a number of good men under that system the scheme did not work out satisfactorily with the steamship companies.
Who got the $25?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He got it,
May I ask the minister if there is similar co-eperation in the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The distributing agent in the country districts is at liberty to use his own judgment. He communicates with our agents in the old country, he tells them there are so many men required in his locality. If a farmer desires to do so, he can avail himself of the services of the employment agent to advance the fare for a man that he wants to bring over. But that is not a part of our system, that is a transaction between the farmer and the employment agent. That is not a part of our business. If the employment agent and the farmer can arrange it between themselves, we have no objection.

The minister will remember that before the Christmas holidays I brought to his attention a matter relating to this very point. A gentleman in Winnipeg, Mr; Hutchings, in the saddleTy business, had completed a large factory, and he wanted to get a number of operators. The saddlery business in England was dull on account of automobiles taking the places of horses and carriages. He could get good men, but these men could not comply with the provisions of the law which required that they should have so much money in their pocket on landing. The explanation the minister gave at the time, I think, was to the effect that the employer could advance the money. I mentioned the fact to Mr. Hutchings, who seemed to be much annoyed, and thought he was not well treated, and he did not agree with the minister as to the facts. I think the minister said there was an obligation which would prevent them from entering with another man's money in their pockets. Perhaps the minister could make his position clear now\

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There must have been some misunderstanding on the part of Mr. Hutchings. There is no objection to Mr. Hutchings or any one else advancing money to men in England. It is none of our business how the man in England gets his money so long as he comes to Canada with the money in his pocket, and we are
satisfied it is his money. We do not care if he has to pay it back afterwards, but if he comes to Canada with the money in his pocket to spend as he pleases, then we are satisfied that he has $25 that will, keep him from becoming a public charge until he has a reasonable opportunity of getting work. But we do object to the employer furnishing that money to him at the port of landing, because the inference is that it is only handed to the immigrant to enable him to pass our officer, and then he must hand it back to the agent who is employing him. That is contrary to our policy, and we do not allow it if we can prevent it. But if the man leaves England with the money in his pocket, we do not concern ourselves whether it was advanced to him or not.

Suppose the employer of labour here has advanced that money to a hundred different men in different places, and they are able to show the money at the port of entry. Well, if there is an obligation to pay it back, could a conscientious man with the money that, was advanced to him for that purpose, and which he knew was not his own, and which had to be earned subsequently, could he make a declaration that that was his money? Then it would be useless to advance him the money. That was the point that Mr. Hutchings made to me.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that is rather straining the point. I cannot imagine many men having so tender a conscience as to be unwilling to say that the money they were entitled to spend as they pleased was not their own money. As a matter of fact, it was their own money.
So the employer has got to make a gift of it, and cannot demand it back subsequently?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He can lend them the money, but the transaction must be made on the other side before he leave*. We do not ask whether the man has to pay the money back or not; the point is that he must have the money, and that he is privileged to spend it as he pleases. If he gets it in England and brings it with him across the ocean, that is evidence that he has had the money in his possession, and the ability to spend it if he wanted to. Therefore, we are satisfied that when he comes to this side he is able to spend it if he "wants to. But if the employer is not willing to give him the money until he lands on this side, that is evidence to us that the employer is not willing to trust him with the money, and the chances are that the money is only given to him to be handed back, and, therefore, it did not belong to the immigrant.
J
I have great respect for the minister, but I have not much respect for the law that he lays down. Even if the money is loaned to him, he still has it in his pocket.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The requirement is that the man who lands in Canada shall not be under the necessity of appealing to charity in case he is not able to find remunerative employment immediately upon landing. Now that is one purpose, and that purpose is served if the man has the money in his pocket when he lands, and can do with it as he pleases, no matter whether he bor-. rows it or not. But if it is only given to him as he lands, and must be handed back to the employer the moment he passes our officer, then that is not his money to do with as he pleases, and is no protection to the immigrant.

It seems that this is not a good law in so far as we are concerned. I understand that we have been endeavouring to secure the very best settlers we are able to get from the British possessions. In this case under discussion, these men were mechanics, they were under contract, they were coming out here with permanent employment assured in Mr. Hutchings' factory. I think the law is-I will not say a silly law-but one that is bound to work to the detriment of our country in preventing us from securing a very desirable class of men. I do not think it is wise in a case of this kind to exact the qualification of having $25 in their pockets. I think men leaving England, Ireland and Scotland, especially mechanics, or any other kind of men that come to this country with assured positions, should not be required to comply with that qualification. Mr. Hutchings complained very bitterly, and he stated that he had a factory that would give employment to four or five hundred men. He told me that he had three hundred mechanics employed to go into that factory, and that these men were refused entry into Canada because they did not hacii have $25 in their pockets. Outside of this case altogether I think the principle is wrong. I think the minister is quite right to apply it to immigrants from foreign countries, Slavs and settlers of that kind, but when you are bringing into this country our own people, because we look upon people from Great Britain as our own people, you should not put such a barrier between them and Canada. If men are enabled to come out here with employment assured there should be no barrier. I can understand that it is necessary to keep out paupers, but there is no danger where men are assured a position, and a responsible man in Canada notifies the department that these men are about to enter his employ. I think the law is a mistaken one when applied in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The law is made to meet a certain condition, it is made for a certain purpose and when the need of the law exists it is desirable that it should be enforced. I quite appreciate the fact that there are times and conditions when it is not necessary to enforce that law, and during a great part of last summer the conditions were relaxed, so that where a mechanic was coming to assured employment the $25 was not insisted upon. But that was during the summer season and when the winter season came we felt that under winter conditions in Canada it was not in the best interests of the country that a man, even if he were coming to what was called assured employment, should come without money in his pocket, because we all know that labour conditions are entirely different in the winter from what they are in the summer, and that if a man is thrown out of employment in the winter he has not the same chance to get employment as in the summer. Although a man may come to assured employment we have no certainty that he will continue in his employment. He may be inefficient, he may have been mistaken in the class of work that he was required to do and the employer would not be warranted in keeping him. Such a man under' such circumstances arriving in the dead of winter will be just as hungry if he is >ut of a job as if he had not been a mechanic or a desirable settler and will become an object of charity. Therefore, we withdrew the relaxation in the fall and it was not until the relaxation had been withdrawn that our friend, Mr. Hutchings, arrived at the conclusion that he needed these men. If he had thought of it a little sooner he would have been able to have got them in without their having the $25; in fact, if I remember aright the relaxation was still in force when my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart, Winnipeg) spoke in the House, and I so informed him.
No, the hon. gentleman is mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the relaxation was in force until the 10th December.
He could not take advantage of it by that time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That may be; I cannot say as to that, but if Mr. Hutchings had arrangements made for his men at the time my hon. friend brought the complaint before the House there was no bar whatever to him getting them in. But, on the 10th December the relaxation was withdrawn, and I appeal to the committee if it is not right and reasonable that during the winter months in Canada any man landing in Canada should be in a position to support himself for a little time at any rate without appealing to any one.

The minister has given us quite a rehearsal; he has spoken particularly of what has been happening in this financial year, and no person in this House outside of himself has any opportunity of investigating any thing in connection with it. Then ihere is another thing that I think we are more interested in perhaps than the numbers he has given us as representing the immigrants who have come into this country. There are only certain classes for which the government are giving bonuses of $5 each to agents. I understand they are farmers, farm labourers and domestic servants. He has told us that they placed over 6,000 in Ontario and Quebec last year, or two-thirds of all they got in of that class. I have here a statement that was made by Mr. Scott, the immigration commissioner. He said that during 1910 we received 9,813 farmers and farm labourers for whom we paid $49,065, that we received 6,015 women for whom we paid a bonus of $30,075 and that we received 2,840 children for whom we paid ten shillings per head, the total amounting to $86,240. As I understand the government's position on this question, it is that they are not supposed to assist any other than these three classes to come to Canada-farmers,, farm labourers and female domestic servants. We have 3,000 agents who are paid commissions for getting immigrants, we have nine regular salaried agents in the old country and during last season we sent over forty special agents at a very great cost. We did not accomplish very much. My own impression is that sending over special agents is a farce. It is very nice for a friend who is in ill-health or who wants a trip to go over as a special immigration agent, get $100 a month and expenses. Some of these expenses are exceedingly high. We keep no track as far as I know of the people who leave the country. The minister told us this afternoon that we got 103,000 immigrants from the United States. If you look at the immigration report of the United States you will find at page 142 the figures given with reference to the year's immigration from the United States to Canada and the emigration from Canada to the United States as follows: Immigrants from United States to Canada-
United States citizens	 78,697
Canadian citizens	 15,203
Aliens	 22,477
Total	116,377
Immigrants from Canada to the United States-
United States citizens	 22,832
Canadian citizens	 44,328
Aliens	 27,336
Total	 94,496
According to the American statement therefore we had the better of them by
21,496 people. It seems to me there is something very strange about this. We have been told that the exodus has been stopped and that our people are not now going to the United States, but here the American statistics show that Canadians are going in large numbers to the neighbouring republic. Now, to get this number of people from the United States, we spent something over $232,347 according to the answer given to me by the minister a; few days ago.
For 21,000 people.

For a little over 21,000 people. Then, there is a discrepancy between the (immigration Teport given out by the department and Lord Strathcona's report to the department. The department says we got from Great Britain and Ireland, 59,760 immigrants last year, while Lord Strathcona says we got 66,554 and strange to say, that while we are told it would cost too much to keep track of the people who leave this country so that statistics might be prepared with regard to them, yet Lord Strathcona in his report to the department at page 65 says:
Some interesting instances of the volume and character of the immigrants from the United Kingdom to Canada, and the return movement to Great Britain from the Dominion are shown by the figures quoted below which have been obtained from official sources.
Then he says there were sent to Canada 113,315 and there returned to the old country 46,791, leaving, as he says, the balance of 66,524. I should like to know why the department does not adopt some system by which we can know the number and character of the people^ who come to this country, as well as of those who leave this country, because unless we have such information, we are entirely in the dark and we are paying out such large sums of money that I think it is time to ary a halt. From 1897 to 1910 we paid out for immigration $8,847,272.33, and if you add the appropriation for this year which amounts to $1,066,250, you will have $9,913,522.33 expended for immigration from 1897 up to the end of the fiscal year. When we remember that the federal government of the United States has not now and never had an immigrant agent, and' when we remember that transportation companies are forbidden under a heavy penalty to solicit immigration, (it is a remarkable thing that last year the United States got over one million one hundred thousand immigrants on whom they collected a head tax of $4 each amounting to over $4,000,000, and they spent for the purpose of keeping out of the country-I thlink that describes

it exactly-$2,631,538, leaving them a balance collected on immigrants for that year amounting to $1,533,428. Now, it is strange to me that while we have 3,000 agents in Great Britain and Ireland, and 45 immigrant agents on commission in the United States and 17 on salary, we are not as successful in proportion as is the American Republic. I would call the special attention of the minister to this point, because I think the time has come when there should be a reduction in the amount of money we are spending, especially when we are getting such meagre results in the line of desirable immigrants. I am sure the minister would hardly like to go before a Trades Union and tell them he brought in about 300,000 immigrants last year, only about 10 per cent of whom were farmers, farm labourers, and domestic servants, notwithstanding that the Trades Unions are opposed to bringing in mechanics and the labour unions are opposed to bringing in labourers and the government declares it is their policy not to bring them in. During the last three years the government has spent over $1,000,000 a year for immigration although when we were in power the Liberal party found very great fault with our expending $120,000 a year for the same purpose. Now, I have figures here from the American report at page 55 which tend to prove that we are getting into Canada a great many undesirable immigrants and that the selection made on the other side before they start for this country is not nearly as perfect as that made by the United States. I may state that in 1907 there was a large convention held in New York at which persons of various notions about immigration met, and prominent citizens of the United States discussed the question thoroughly. That same year the Congress of the United States passed a law appointing a commission to investigate the whole matter of immigration and the commission was permitted to go anywhere it chose to pursue its investigation, and to report the result. They say, in an interim summary report, that their complete report will require about 40 volumes, and while I do not expect the Minister of the Interior to read the whole 40 volumes, yet I think it would well repay him to read the summary report presented by the commission. Now, in the figures given below it is shown beyond peradventure, that the United States were called upon to reject fewer immigrants on this side of the Atlantic than Canada rejected, and the reason for that is that the process of selection on the other side before the immigrants start for the American continent, is much more perfect under the United States system than under ours. I quote the following figures: Mr. WILSON (Lennox and Addington).

If this statement is true, it shows a great laxity on the part of our Immigration Department in allowing undesirable immigrants to embark for this country. I am informed that the United States have medical officers in some of the European countries for the past ten years. I believe we have one in New York; I do not know that we have any other. Then, every captain of a vessel bringing immigrants to the United States must make a declaration on reaching port that the medical officer of the ship has examined every immigrant on board, both orally and otherwise, and when they land, the medical officer on shore has to do the same thing. It is said that there are often as many rejected at the port of embarkation as are brought over. The shipping companies have got tired of carrying people both ways for one fare. Besides, if any contagious disease is found among the immigrants that might have been discovered before the ship sailed, the shipping companies are liable to a fine of $100, besides having to take back the affected people to the country from which they came. I made some mention of that last year when the Immigration Bill was before the House, and did what I could to assist in improving that measure. I wanted to have it made as stringent as possible, because I look upon the immigration business as the most important business we have in this country. If we bring into the country a lot of people who are weaklings or insane, we can never correct the mistake, whereas if we spend a little more money on anything than we should, we have only to work a little harder to make up the loss. In the Ontario report on the hospitals for the insane for last year, it is stated that during ten months of that year 168 insane persons were sent back, and that was a saving to the province of $400,000, I suppose taking into account the number of years that these people would have to be maintained if they had been left here. That I think shows that our immigration regulations are too lax. One thing the department has done which I am pleased with, although it costs a good deal of money. It has appointed, along our border, between Canada and the United States, 69 regular preventive officers to prevent undesirable people coming into this country. In addition, I understand, there are 132 customs officers who are required to act as preventive officers for the same purpose. That makes an army of a little over 200, and while it is a little expensive, these people render a valuable service. The department

has sent a number of people to the old country as farmer delegates, and it seems to value them all the same, because it pays them all the same salary, except one lady, who is paid at a much higher rate than the others. Donald Irwin, from Lloyd-minster, Saskatchewan, was employed for four months at $100 a month, and was paid $761.50 for expenses, or over $6.25 per day. Alexander D. Gamby, from Griswold, Manitoba, was paid a salary of $100 a month for three months, and $606.16 for expenses, or about $6.70 per day. S. Larcombe, of Birtle, Manitoba, was paid $100 a month for three months, and $718.28 for expenses, or about $7.98 per day. Rev. J. A. Winfield, of St. Stephen, New Brunswick, was paid $100 a month for four months and $742.68 for expenses, or almost $6 per day. J. G. Turgeon, of Hardisty, Saskatchewan, was paid $100 a month for five months and $885.47 for expenses, or $5.90 per day. Agnes D. Cameron of England was paid $200 a month for four months and $2,592.62 for expenses, or $21.60 per day. H. S. Bardal, of Winnipeg, was paid $100 a month for six months and $1,143.43 for expenses, or $6.35 per day. William Griffith, of St. John, New Brunswick, was paid $100 a month for eight months and $1,613.84 for expenses, or $201.73 per month. That there may be no mistake about this matter, I will read the heading of the statement which Mr. Scott sent to the committee: ' Farmer delegates sent to the British Isles and Europe, fiscal year 1909-10.' I do not know the position this lady, Agnes D. Cameron, occupies, but I can hardly imagine that she is properly described as a farmer delegate. I think the time has come when we should cry a halt in spending money so recklessly in connection with immigration, and for getting into the country many people whom we do not want. What we do want are farmers, farm labourers and female domestics; but I do not think the government can take credit for bringing in a lot of other people who prefer to live in the cities and towns. The United States reports show that about 40 per cent of the immigrants go home again and about 30 per cent stay when they do go. This indicates that the immigrants who are going to the United States now are not the same kind that came years ago. Formerly they came to become citizens and make homes for themselves and throw in their lot with the people of the country. Now many come during the good times when they can get good wages, and then it is so easy to go back that they return home again and take their money with them. I would like the minister to give us a pledge to-night that he will look into this matter and see if he cannot curtail the wasteful expenditure that is taking place on immigration at the present time.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity of making a few remarks in regard to immigration.
In providing the means for starting an overwhelming influx of immigrants with the object of developing our resources, we have too often neglected to lay down strict rules for the proper selection of such immigrants. Accordingly people have been admitted whose character was not always above reproach.
In the course of the last session, parliament and the government materially improved the law in this respect. However, the form to be filled in and signed by the immigrant is not of a nature to enlighten us as to the latters' character.
The hon. minister should require from the immigrants a certificate vouching for their good behaviour. Such certificate might be delivered by a magistrate, by the physician attending the immigrant, by the clerk of a court, by a clergyman or by the mayor of the municipality wherein the immigrant resides. Such a formality might be readily complied with. Desirable citizens wouid be proud to hand to the proper officers a certificate giving evidence of their good behaviour. It would be an honourable certificate of registration for each new citizen of Canada.
Last session, I applied for the correspondence which had taken place between the medical immigration inspectors and the superintendent of immigration. I made a special study of the methods of medical inspection followed at Quebec. I appreciate the learning and the zeal of Dr. Page, superintendent of the immigration hospital and head of the inspection service at Quebec. I foresee that in the near future satisfactory results will be forthcoming from his work, his researches and his suggestions.
I wish to make a passing reference to the annual report of the Department of the Interior. The hon. minister publishes only the.reports of our inspectors, of our immigration agents and the reports of our agents in the British Isles, in France and in Belgium. Unfortunately these reports are oftentimes a mere rehash of the facts already in print. They do not impart any information in respect to our colonization societies or our agents in the New England states. I hope that henceforth the hon. minister will cause to be included in his annual report an account of the work done by all our immigration agents.
We are seeking to blend with our native-born population swarms of foreign elet-ments. We cannot be too careful in the selection of these outsiders. The United States, though their population aggregates 90,000,000, are fearful lest they may be unable to cope with such large arrivals of immigrants, and they are endeavouring by means of restrictive legislation to impede

the rush into the country of immigrants from foreign lands.
The Canadianization of foreign elements in this young country of ours, with its immense territory, presents a social problem of the greatest importance. The growing generations of immigrants, constantly increasing, may ultimately have the upper hand in the management of our affairs. It is then incumbent on us to make^ a most judicious selection of these immigrants. Some political men conceive the greatest fears in regard to the proposed trade reciprocity arrangements between Canada and the United States. They fear the effects of an immigration policy which has attracted to Canada since 1900 close on one million immigrants from the United States. In their opinion, Canadian feeling is not sufficiently developed, is not sufficiently strong, does not exert enough prestige, to allow us safely to go into a business understanding of that kind with our neighbours. But I cannot admit that such an arrangement implies the slightest weakening of our feelings of loyalty towards the mother country.
It is with sadness that I see so many of our Canadians leaving this country for the United States.
Hon. Mr. LEMIEUX (Translation.) Do you mean French Canadians?
Mr. PAQUET (Translation.) I said Canadians.
Mr. MARTIN (Translation.) What about those who are coming back to Canada?
Mr. PAQUET (Translation.) Statistics go to show that during the fiscEtl year 1908-09, 18,111 Canadians emigrated to the United States for good. In 1908-09, that figure reached 43,805. During the last fiscal year, 53,448 Canadians left to take up their homes in the United States. According to the report of Mr. Rene Dupont, immigration agent at Quebec, 19,000 French Canadians have left the province of Quebec. Over 11,000 emigrated to the United States. Such figures should induce us to make untiring and strenuous efforts towards keeping in the country the sons of Canada.

If the Dominion government is intent on attaining that goal, they should hasten to reorganize the office of our general agent Mr. PAQUET.
in France. We should have at Paris, as our representative, an active, able mart, thoroughly versed in business matters. We should so arrange that this agency of ours in France may become a powerful means of extending our trade, a centre whence Canadian energy may radiate with irresistible force. As a matter of fact, even a cursory acquaintance with the course of immigration in Canada, within the last few years especially, will satisly one as to this:	while during a period of fifteen or
twejity years we may at times have shown too much leniency toward immigrants entering Canada, for the last five or six years, and more particularly within the last two years we have made the regulations such that to-day we can natter ourselves with having an immigration practically above reproach.
I shall recall to my hon. friend clauses 40 and 41 of the regulations concerning immigration, and he will aver that under these two clauses and subsection 2 of clause 42, the minister is vested with full powers, that is with unrestricted autocratic powers as regards the deportation of immigrants branded as undesirable.
There is no doubt that Canada leads among the countries of the world in looking after immigrants with a view to retaining only the best. It is almost out of the question for an immigrant with some criminal offence chargeable against him or some dark spot in his record to get into Canada, considering that very stringent regulations await him on arrival. I was happy to gather from what my hon. friend said that he gave credit to the government for having done their duty in that respect.
I shall now pass to another point raised by the hon. gentleman. He called the attention of the House to the exit of Canadian emigrants to the New England states. He will agree with me, I think, that in the course of the last fifteen years we have succeeded in checking that exit. He will admit that fifteen or twenty years ago our rural communities were rapidly being depopulated. At the time I travelled through the province of Quebec and I knoto well that in certain back settlements, and even in the streets of extensive villages, abandoned houses could be pointed to, and they made up one quarter, if not one half of the total, their occupiers having left for the United States. But to-day, thank God, when our fellow citizens leave the province of Quebec, it is to settle on the fertile western plains, in Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and even in British Columbia and the Yukon. Only a very small minority, indeed, take to the New England states. They go to work there during the winter months, but they return in the spring to work the land. Of course my hon. friend is well aware that since the building of the Transcontinental has been started, new parishes have been established in the counties of L'Islet, Temiscouata and others on the south shore, new industries spring up at every point where our French Canadian fellow citizens are called upon to play a leading nart.

It seems to me almost incredible that we should have succeeded in developing French immigration to such an extent in the space of so short a period, and I shall explain why I take that view.
I have made a special study of that question, not only in books, but on the spot, in France, as well as of the means the Canadian government had at their disposal. The problem appealed to me, not only as a Canadian, but as a French Canadian, still remindful of his lineage. I considered that we had a right to our share in that great flow of immigration which is pouring from year to year over this continent of our1'. I went to headquarters for my information, and I say to my hon. friend, with the hone that my voice will be heard throughout the province of Quebec, that the directing of a continuous and powerful stream of immigration from France to Canada is practically an impossibility. In the first place, it is admitted that the population of France is decreasing year by year. That is a sad circumstance for our old mother country, but it is the exact truth. In the second place, France is under a regime of compulsory military service; and for these two reasons the French government not only dislikes the idea of Frenchmen emigrating to foreign lands, but frowns on any scheme for recruiting immigrants. Two years ago, I was in Paris shortly after the hon. Mr. Fabre, who was already a sick man at the time, had got communication of a circular sent out from the Department of the Interior in France to prefects, prohibiting all endeavours towards recruiting emigrants for Canada. The French government complained to the British embassy that, notwithstanding regulations to the contrary, our agents in France persisted in carrying on their work. The French government took exception to certain clergymen appointed by the Canadian government travelling through the country with a view to inducing peasants to emigrate to Canada.
They complain also of the activitv of our agents who encourage school teachers to promote emigration to this country. The French Minister of the Interior called the attention of our ambassador to this matte" which he called a grave irregularity. I thereupon called on the Prime Minister Mr. Briand, whom I had the honour of

meeting a few days previously at the Chamber of Deputies and explained to him that our agents did not intend to organize a propaganda, but merely desired to convey to those peasants who desired to emigrate, information which might decide them in favour of Canada. I also left in Mr. Briand's hands a memorandum explaining the nature of instructions given to our agents, and he promised to look into the matter carefully with a view to a future conference.
Some few months ago, I was again in Paris, and in order to make it clear to the committee that it is impossible to us to undertake any propaganda in Prance, I will state that another circular was placed in my hands, it having been, this time, delivered to our commissioner through the channel of the British Embassy. I carefully read that circular; it confirms the opinion just now expressed by me that the government will not permit any kind of emigration propaganda on the part of Canada or of any other coutnry.
Mr. PAQUET (Translation.) Had that circular been altered?
Hon. Mr. LEMIEUX (Translation.) It has not been altered. In fact the action of our agents is practically paralyzed, as any efforts in that direction might expose them to a fine and even to deportation.
Another fact must not be forgotten when we are discussing French emigration. How can France encourage her citizens to settle in foreign countries, when her own colonies scarcely receive a sufficient number of French immigrants to counterbalance the foreign element? I read the other day an interesting article published in 'La Revue des Deux Mondes '; it may enlighten my hon. friend from L'Islet.
In that article of ' La Revue des Deux Mondes,' the writer recalled the fact, that in Tunis, a French colony whose climate is similar to that of the South of France and only a few hours distant from Marseilles, the French population is in a proportion of 25 per cent, while the Italian element represents 75 per cent; I mean, of course, of the white population, not the native. France being unable to people Tunis, her most valuable colony, how can she encourage her citizens to settle in Canada or in America?
Of course, with due exercise of tact and discretion, our agents in France may be able to direct towards Canada those Frenchmen who have in any case decided to come to America. But as to supposing that any large number of such emigrants may be obtained, that would be an illusion. We may consider ourselves lucky to have been able during the last decade, to increase so materially the figures of French immigration; but once again I sav let us not count upon any large increase. As to Belgium, the case is different. The Belgium government is less opposed to an emigration propaganda, yet it must be carried on with due discretion. Besides we must not forget-that Belgium is an exceedingly wealthy country and that from such countries emigration is usually limited. Nevertheless, thanks to the Minister of Agriculture, our pavillion at Brussels was the central point of attraction at the last World's Fair. Hundreds of thousands of Belgians have been able to read and study our circulars, atlases and folders published both in French and Flemish describing the wealth and beauty of this land. I am convinced that in consequence of that exhibit, several thousands of Belgian colonists will settle here. It is easier to carry on a propaganda by means of these exhibitions than by agents. Besides such agents are excluded not from France and Belgium merely but from every important country in Europe. In the United Kingdom alone complete liberty of canvass is allowed. In Germany and Russia emigration propaganda is forbidden. Two or three years ago a Russian officer who was quite familiar with conditions obtaining in Germany and Russia, informed me that he could secure for us several thousands of excellent immigrants, I introduced him to the Minister of the Interior who was quite willing to authorize his work in Lithuania, provided he first obtained permission from the Russian and German governments to carry on the work. The officer consulted the Russian and German consuls, and both informed him that their respective governments would forbid anything of this kind. All this tends to establish that it is quite impossible to undertake any such propaganda in violation of the precise instructions given by the authorities either to the prefects or to the governors of provinces. England alone gives us a free hand.
My hon. friend has expressed some fear as to the future of our country. He believes that we are being invaded by Americans and he considers that theTe is danger of a change in the mental trend of the Canadian people. In my opinion that is a mistake, and the fears expressed by my hon. friend are groundless.
Mr. PAQUET (Translation.) I quoted those words vfrom certain statesmen who feared such a result, but I said that, for my part, I did not believe that the proposed commercial agreement would interfere with our attachment to the mother land.

my presence that they are quite mistaken. It is not so much the true Americans that come to Canada as Germans, Scandinavians and even Canadians who had emigrated to the United States.

I cannot give a satisfactory explanation of the discrepancy offhand. I ask my hon. friend to give ine an opportunity to go into the accounts and see on which side the error is. Although Miss Cameron's salary appears m the list of salaries of farm delegates, she is not a Mr. LEMIEUX.
farm delegate. The farm delegate is a practical, successful farmer, if possible, of British birth, who is sent, if possible, to the part of the country from which he came. He is not expected or required to be a man of many words, but he is expected and required to be a man of material success, so that when he goes to the place of his birth in the old country and meets his friends, and they ask him what he has done, he will have something to tell them-not what he thinks, or has heard, or believes, or supposes, but what he has done in the way of material success. He is in himself an example to the old countryman of what may be achieved in Canada. For these reasons we do not look for men who have any particular ability in speaking, lecturing or making an appearance before the public. But it is necessary to have also lecturers, people who have the ability to interest audiences by delivering addresses. Miss Cameron has a reputation as a lecturer and also a writer. She is a native-born Canadian, a native of British Columbia, has travelled a great deal in Canada, and has had a great deal of experience both as a writer and as a lecturer. We did not think we were making a mistake-and we do not think so now-in retaining her services at the price paid. We could not expect to retain the services of an experienced writer and lecturer at the same rate as a larmer who had no such experience and qualifications.
Was Miss Cameron a farmer?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have just explained that she is a lecturer, a lady of Canadian birth who has travelled a great deal in Canada and knows a great deal of the various provinces, and also has the ability to tell what she has seen and what she knows in such a manner as to be interesting to the listener.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I feel very strongly on the point that the money that Canada pays to induce immigration should be paid with particular attention to getting the kind of people we want and need in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In regard to the farm delegates, of whom my hon. friend seems to think so little, he is only one means of trying to reach the actual farmer. Now, I cannot think of any way that is more likely to reach the actual farmer in the old country than sending the actual farmer in Canada to meet him. If the experience of the successful farmer in Canada will not appeal to the successful farmer in the old country-who is a man we want-I do not know any argument that will. The old country farmer, as every one knows, is very conservative in his ideas-very slow to move-he would not be half so good a man as he is if he could be moved easily. It will take time to get a movement amongst these people; but we believe we have taken the right course and that we are starting the movement. It is well known that English and Scotch farmers are the best farmers in the world, and this country needs as many of these people as we can get. And I can conceive of no better way to reach the old country farmer than by sending the successful Canadian farmer to tell him what he has been doing.

I moved for a return of the reports of these farm delegates. I am sorry to say that in the whole return there was not a single report from one of them. Mr. Walker wrote a little letter about one, some man had given some lectures, another man interviewed a number of people and they expected great results. If we could get returns from these gentlemen to show what they are doing for the money they get it would be of some use. I have not for some years moved for that because the last time' I moved for it it was so unsatisfactory I did not think it was worth while.

I listened to what the minister said. I am not a farmer, but I understand the hon. gentleman to argue that the old country farmer is a very conservative individual and hard to move or convince. The minister's theory is that the best way to convince the old country farmer is to send to him a man whom he does not know, a Canadian farmer. I would think the best way to convince the old country farmer would be to get some trustworthy people from there to come here and see what our farming means. Such a man would be far more likely to influence him than the paid employee of this government, and the last person who would be likely to influence such a conservative old country farmer would be a young lady like this Miss Cameron to whom the minister pays a handsome salary, and who deliver lectures on farming in Canada. I'o suppose that she can convince the doubtful farmer is nonsense.

The minister told us that the English and Scotch farmers were the best in the world. I am not prepared to combat that argument with any evidence, but I am surprised to learn that these old country farmers can succeed any better in Canada than our Canadian farmers. I wish the minister would go over and watch the operations of these men and then I fancy he would not make such an invidious comparison as he has made with reference to our Canadian farmers. I would like to know what the minister has done to dissipate the idea prevalent in the old country that this country is so cold and that our people have to work so hard. Do the lectures delivered there give any evidence of the teni-perature? From my experience in talking with men in Scotland I would think something of that kind was necessary. I was able to tell them that while our temperature may not be as moderately warm as theirs, still we have sunshine_ which I think makes up for the degree -of leisure that they have in the old country. My impression is that the man who gets along here in farming has to work pretty hard. It was a surprise to me to find that the minister was sending farmers from this country who are not as good farmers as those in the old land to instruct them what to do. The minister will have to get a better class of men than the Canadian farmers to instruct these people, if he still adheres to the idea that the Scotch or English farmer is better than the Canadian.

Are there any efforts being made to bring immigrants into the unsettled portions of Ontario? speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far the government has not taken up the question of colonization in northern Ontario. We have, however taken an interest in the colonization of what might be called far western Ontario. We have an agent at Port Arthur, who looks after the Rainy River country, and who has been employed there for seven or eight years. We have not taken up the question of the settlement of northern Ontario for the reason that until the Grand Trunk Pacific is in operation, the clay belt which has been spoken of so much is not available for settlement. There is land along the line of the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway between North Bay and Co.chrane, but I do not know that the field for settlement there is sufficiently desirable to warrant the government in making any special effort. But as soon as the clay belt is made available by the construction of the Transcontinental and its operation, no doubt the government will be ready to take up the question of directing colonization into that part of the country.
