Seaport expenses at Halifax, St. John, Sydney, Quebec, Montreal, Victoria, Vancouver and Prince Rupert, $20,000. This is to provide for the general expenses of the port officers and officials, covering expenses of meeting boats and trains, temporary assistance, uniforms, maintenance of immigration halls and general office expenses. The expenditure for the fiscal year
1909-10 was $17,641.25, and for the six months ended September 30, 1910, $13,200.84.
Commissions for locating farm help and domestic servants, $4,000. This is to pay for commissions to agents appointed in Ontario and Quebec for placing farm labourers and domestic servants at the rate of $2 for each person so placed.
The expenditure for 1909-10 was $3,923.50, and for the six months ended September 30, 1910, $2,542.60.
General expenses of officials in connection with deportation of undesirable immigrants, $15,000. This is to provide for the travelling and living expenses of officials accompanying persons deported, and also for expenses of deportees. Whenever such expenses are borne by a transportation company a refund of same is obtained from the company. The following officials are employed in connection with this service: R.. Boston, P. Devlin, R. Dow, A. Blanchet, C. Choquette, Mrs. M. Killeen and Mrs. E. Tasse. The expenditure for 1909-10 was $15,905.91, and for the six months ended September, 30, 1910, $6,201.15.
Telegrams, telephones, freight and express charges at head office, $7,000. The expenditure for these services for the fiscal year 1909-10 was $8,797.15, and for the six months ended September 30, 1910, $3,242.57.
Medical services and supplies $3,000. This is to meet the expenditure for treatment of immigrants at the various immi-164
gration halls at the eastern and western ports and at Winnipeg. The expenditure for 1909-10 was $869.24, and for the six months ended September 30, 1910, $1,588.50.
What was the last statement-treating patients?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Treating immigrants at various immigration halls.
Outside of Winnipeg? Mr. OLIVER. Yes.
At Winnipeg they have a regular physician paid a salary?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a special vote for Winnipeg^ which goes to the hospital and the hospital attends to the treatment of the immigrants.
I understand that, but have you not a physician in Winnipeg paid a salary to treat immigrants?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a salaried physician at the immigration hall.
Why should there be extra treatment in Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There formerly was a hospital in connection with the hall, .but we found it was better and more economical to arrange with the hospitals to treat patients and so the medical man has simply to diagnose the cases.
The next item covers that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Then what is this amount for treating patients?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is at places outside of Winnipeg.
And does not touch anything in Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No.
Customs duty, $1,000.
This is to provide for customs duty and customs brokers fees' on literature, maps, pamphlets, &c.
Boundary inspection expenses $20,000. This is to cover the expenses of officials employed along the boundary between Canada and the United States for the inspection of immigrants entering Canada. The expenditure during 1909-10 was $59,364.70 (including salaries, which are charged to the salaries vote) and for the six months ended September, 1910, $5,688.87.
Detention hospitals: Halifax, St. John, Quebec, Montreal and Victoria, $10,000.
This is to provide for the equipment and maintenance of the hospitals above named; for the treatment of immigrants who have contracted some minor contagious disease



on ship board, and detention of those not receiving treatment. For every immigrant treated, the rate of $1.25 per day is charged and 50 cents per day for those not under treatment. No charge is made for infants under one year. All the amounts earned at the above rates are collected from the steamship companies who brought the immigrants to Canada.
Farmer delegates, $35,000.
This is to cover the salaries and expenses of delegates sent to the old country in the interest of immigration. The men so engaged are all practical and successful farmers. The expenses during 1909-10 were $36,076.57.
Locating settlers in the west, $65,000.
This amount is to cover the expenditure to be made by the commissioner of immigration at Winnipeg, for locating settlers in the west. The bulk of this expenditure is comprised of:
Salaries and expenses of interpreters, land guides, temporary agents and clerks, caretakers, &c.; of contingencies of the Winnipeg and other agencies in the west, including postage, telephones, telegrams, advertising, provisions, and supplies for needy immigrants, homesteaders, equipment, maintenance of halls, uniforms and travelling expenses of officials.
The expenditure for 1910 was $59,766.30 and for six months ended 30th September, 1910, $29,483.36.
Collection of exhibits, $20,000.
This is to cover expenditure in connection with the purchase of fine specimens of fruit, grain and vegetables grown in Canada, to be used as exhibits in the offices of our agents; at fairs in United States; in the offices of our agents and on motor cars in Great Britain. This is thought to be one of the best means of advertising Canada and experience has proved that the sight of those fine exhibits has influenced many to settle in this country. The expenditure for 1909-10 was $23,429.13 and for six months ended 30th September, 1910, $2,449.76.
Contingencies and general expenses in the United States, $60,000.
This is to provide for the travelling expenses of our agents and their living expenses while travelling, especially while attending at fairs; for rent of offices, temporary assistance, telegrams, telephones, postage, office furniture and general expenses of the various offices in the United States. The expenditure for 1909-10 was $64,319.06, and for six months ended 30th September, 1910, $33,922.59.
Commissions on settlers from United States, $9,000.
This is to provide for the payment of commissions to local agents employed in Mr. OLIVER.
the United States who issue settlers' certificates which entitle the holders to transportation at a reduced rate of one cent per mile over the Canadian Pacific Tailway, Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern railways. These certificates are returned to the department by the railway companies and commissions are paid to the various agents who issue them at the following rates: $3 peT male; $2 per female and $1 per child under 18 years of age. The expenditure for 1909-10 was $3,900.75 and for six months ended September 30, 1910, $2,162.
British bonuses, $57,000.
Bonuses allowed as follows: fl on each person 18 years of age or over and 10 shillings on those between 1 and 18 years of age. The expenditure for 1909-10 was $39,145.65 and for six months ended September 30, 1910, $47,989.17.
That does not correspond with the evidence given by Mr. Scott. The bonus paid agents in Great Britain and Ireland last year amounted to $86,000, according to Mr. Scott's evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The statement I have quoted is $39,145.65 for 1909-10 and we are asking for $57,000 for this year because they expect a larger immigration of that class of people.
Ia that the amount of money you paid to agents at the rate of $5 per head for adults and 10 shillings for children?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Well, the statement is certainly greatly at variance with that made by Mr. Scott. There were about
18,000	people that the bonus was earned on last year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The number of people does ru t give you the amount, because some would be children and some adults. I have a copy of Mr. Scott's statement here, and I will turn it up in a moment. My statement here is that the expenditure for 1909-10 was $39,145.65 and for the six months ended September 30, 1910, $47,989.17.
That is bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Bonus actually paid.
For farmers, farm labourers and domestics?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and we are asking for the same service for the coming year $57,000.

Is it not so that quite a number of these men who have come out and upon whom the bonuses have been

paid, as farm labourers, have gone to work on railways?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is quite passible.
That would hardly be the proper designation for them would it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, it would not, but in so far as we are aware, the payment is only made on those who go into domestic service or farm labour. If we find that a man upon whom the bonus is claimed, has gone to railway work, and not farm labour, we do not pay the bonus, or if we have paid the t onus already, we deduct it from the nexo claim made by that agent.
How long does it run for?
How many cases have they found where a farm labourer was really a railway workman going to work upon a contract, and how much was deducted on that account?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be impossible to answer that offhand without having an opportunity to get the details in the department.
Are there any such cases?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly there are.
You found that a number brought out ostensibly as settlers have been really* brought out to work on railways?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, but they have gone to work upon railways.

I have looked into the matter, and I am quite sure that a large number of these have never done anything else, but work upon the railways and I have reason to believe that as soon as they finished working upon the railways they went back again. If the hon. gentleman says that his department has investigated and deducted the money in such cases or had it refunded, I will be willing to take his word in the meantime.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend absolute assurance as to that.

The statistics show that from July 1, 1900, to March 31, 1910, 497,390 immigrants came from the United States direct. Of course, a considerable number of these might come through the United States from foreign countries and not be United States citizens at all. Is there any information which tells what nationality these people belong to?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We take account of the different nationalities of the people who come from the United States, but we have never published it. VVe have given the 1644
United States credit for all those who come from the United States.
What proportion were born in the United States, and are really United States citizens?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have the statistics as to that, but we have not compiled them, although the officer of the department makes a guess that possibly 50 per cent of them would be born in the United States.
It is misleading to publish that this large number came from the United States when in reality only about half of them are United States citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, the large majority of them are United States citizens naturalized but a considerable proportion were not born in the United States. If it is thought desirable to compile the figures it could be done.
In the United States returns they give the nationalities of those who went over to the United States from Canada.

It is important that we should know the origin of these people who come from the United Stares. For example the Doukhobor and the Norwegian stand on a very different basis, and it is well to know whether out of 100 people who come from the United States we are getting one Norwegian and 99 Doukhobors or the reverse.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Heretofore it was not considered of sufficient interest to compile that information, but it might be done.

I suppose there is no better settler than the Scandinavian, and other people of northern continental Europe, while there is a prejudice against some other nationalities, and it is desirable we should know whether we are getting what we consider the desirable class or the objectionable class.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As a matter of fact the immigration that has come from the United States into western Canada has been chiefly or I might say entirely of the desirable class.
They are mostly Anglo-Saxons.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Or Scandinavian or German. We have an exclusion service now along the frontier which comes in contact with the undesirable class to such an extent that last year we rejected at boundary points over 14,000. But we have not up to the present time considered it important because the people coming to settle on the land were of the desirable class.
Will you try after this to keep track of those who leave the country as well as those who come in?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If it is considered necessary, we will do so, but it would add very considerably to the expense, and I do not know that the information would compensate us for doing so.
Will the minister tell us how Lord Strathcona collected the information that 46,000 returned to the old country of the 113,000 sent out? That statement is on page 65 of the report.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The figures were, I presume, secured by Lord Strathcona from the British Board of Trade, which takes account of all the people going and coming from and to British ports.
How do the Americans get their figures?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They simply keep a sufficiently large staff to enable them to collect these statistics.

If you are going into partnership with them on reciprocity, perhaps it would be as well to do so in regard to these statistics. I want to refer to the bonuses. According to Mr. Scott's evidence, we paid bonuses in 1909-10 on 9,813 men, 6,015 women and 2,840 children. If you multiply the number of the men and women by five and the number of children by half that, you will get the same amount of the bonuses paid. I make it $86,240.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: How are we to know about these matters? The minister gives us the calendar year at one time and the fiscal year at another.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Contingencies and general expenses in Great Britain and Ireland, including the London office, $55,000.
This is to meet the expenditure of the London office and of our agents; for rent of offices, taxes, light, postage, telegrams, furniture, temporary assistance, expenses re motor and exhibition wagons, &c. The expenditure for 1909-10 was $55,073.42 (including salaries), and for the six months ended September, 1910, $21,048.29.
Contingencies and general expenses on continent, $7,000.
This is to cover the expenditure in connection with our offices in France and Belgium, including rent, postage, telegrams, stationery, printing, living and travelling expenses, &c. The expenditure for 1909-10 was $12,009.44 (including salaries and for six months ended September, 1910, $1,062.48 (excluding salaries).
Grants to hospitals in the west (not including Winnipeg and St, Boniface), $4,000.
This is to pay for the difference between the provincial government's grant of 50 cents per day in Alberta and Saskatchewan and 25 cents per day in Manitoba for each patient, less whatever may be collected from the immigrants, and $1 per day which is charged by the hospitals on every destitute bona fide immigrant who is treated before he has been one year in Canada. The following hospitals are granted the allowance above stated; The Calgary, Edmonton, Medicine Hat, Regina, Prince Albert, Brandon and Holy Cross, and the Margaret Scott Nursing Mission. The expenditure for 1909-10 was $2,106.13, and for the six months ended September, 1910, $1,588.50.
Grant to Quebec and Lake St. John railway, $8,000.
The above grant is made in consideration of colonization work carried on by the above company in the Lake St. John district. One of the inducements offered to colonists by this railway is free transportation to every bona fide settler locating in that district. The grant is for same amount as for 1916-11.
Do you also pay a bonus to the agent who causes these people to come?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We pay salaried agents in the United States to induce them to come to the Lake St. John district,
Have you not got in that district men on commission?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, this is the only local aid we give.
Province of Quebec Repatriation and Colonization Society, $4,000.
This society has been doing good work for many years in the interest of immigration in the province of Quebec and north-

ern Ontario. The grant is the same as for
1910-11.
Ottawa Valley Immigration Aid Society, $2,500.
This society is chiefly operating in the Ottawa Valley, distributing immigration literature and pamphlets, and giving each year a series of lectures on the interests of general immigration and colonization. The grant is the same as for 1910-11.
L'Union Nationale Francaise, Montreal,

This is in aid of the above society which has been keeping a house of refuge for quite a number of years, and which makes a special effort to receive, aid and care for French immigrants and to distribute them in various parts of Canada. The grant is the same as has been made for the last six years.
Womens' National Immigration Society, Montreal, $1,500.
This society established a home in Montreal for the purpose of giving aid and caring for female immigrants arriving in that city. The home is comfortable and attractive, and rendering valuable assistance to immigrants in procuring lodging and meals at a very low rate. The grant is the same as for former years.
Womens' Welcome Hostel, Toronto,

This Home was incorporated in 1906 and has for its object the reception and general assistance to immigrant women. One day's board and lodgings is given free, very low rates being charged when remaining longer at the hostel. The grant is the same as for previous years.
The Girls' Home of Welcome, Winnipeg, $750.
The above home was established twelve years ago. The object of the institution is to aid and care for immigrant women and domestic servants. Under agreement with the government, female immigrants coming to the home are given one full day's free board and lodgings. This is the same grant as for the last few years.
The Calgary Womens' Hostel, $500.
The aims and objects of this hostel are similar to the Girls' Home of Welcome in Winnipeg. The grant is the same as for previous years.
Canada West Publicity Office, $5,000.
This is an organization of business men of Western Canada and United States, promoting immigration from the western states. Their mode of operation is by having special articles on immigration to western Canada published in newspapers circulated in western states, the aggregate circulation of which amounts to over thirty-four millions in the year 1909-1910. The Canadian Pacific, Grand Trunk and Canadian Northern railways each make a similar grant to this organization. The grant is the same as for 1910-11.	,11
Salvation Army grants, $15,516.66.
This is to cover the different amounts granted to the Salvation Army to help that organization to carry on their good work in the interests of immigration, for the rent of London, (England) office, $4,866.66; advertising in the Salvation Army publications, $2,433.33; special articles in the 'Emigration Gazette ', $1,216.67; allowance for distribution of immigrants and domestic servants in Canada, $7,000.
Miscellaneous and unforeseen expenses, $1,233.34.
Total contingencies and expenses for
1911-12, $700,000.
The Canada West publicity office is aided not merely by the government, but, as I have indicated, by the three great railway companies as weil. This institution conducts a publicity campaign in the United States through newspapers and magazines. Instead of an ordinary advertisement, an article dealing with the publication of articles setting forth Canada's advantages, is secured in different publications in the United States. It is not an ordinary advertising propaganda, but it is very useful.
The three railways have joined in this?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They co-operate with the government. Each of the four organizations pays $5,000. The accounts are audited by the railway and the vouchers-that is, the articles clipped from the papers, are furnished to and audited by them.

What percentage of the large expenditure on advertising, lecturers and so on, is devoted to directing immigration to British Columbia? i am not sure of the position now, but a year or two ago a great many of the lecturers practically ignored the existence of British Columbia. I may tell the minister that it is exceedingly important that we should get all the immigration possible. The labour situation has been rather acute during the last two or three years, and it is getting more acute every year, especially in fruit growing districts. Many of the agents sent over to lecture on Canada have been absolutely ignorant of the conditions in British Columbia. I remember, on one occasipn, when in England, I listened to a representative of Australia, who was declaiming vigorously on the advantages of immigrants going to that country rather than to Canada. He spoke of the extremely severe conditions of the Canadian winter, and said that cattle had to be kept housed up for six months of the year, and even then frequently starved to death. I asked him if he would be surprised to know that within a hundred and fifty miles of my home was a place where, to my knowledge.
12,000	head of cattle were kept by one company, and these cattle never had shelter at all. He asked me where this was, and I

told him in British Columbia. His answer was: That maj be in British Columbia, but not in Canada. I found a great many like that of those who should have given information about British Columbia to people anxious to obtain it, and it seems to me important that they should be familiar with the conditions beyond the Rocky mountains. I know that the minister has had one or two good men there, and has also published some pamphlets, but, I should be glad to have some assurance from the minister that his department is paying rauier serious attention to our immigration needs. He knows that in British Columbia we pay a larger share per capita of the Dominion revenues than any other province, and I think that in this matter ot immigration we deserve special consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The conditions in regard to British Columbia are the same as in regard to the older provinces. That is, the attraction of free land ready for cultivation does not exist there as it does in the prairie provinces, and therefore it is not as easy to secure the attention of prospective settlers for British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick or Nova Scotia as for the prairie provinces.

I am aware of that, so far as the actual settler goes who wants to acquire land. I was thinking, however, especially of the large number of labourers on whom the minister pays a bonus and who go on the land to work but not to take up land for themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I intended to cover that point. The main purpose of the immigration effort of the Dominion government, of course, is to bring into cultivation tRe vacant land of the prairie provinces. But, in doing that, we put out literature which covers the whole Dominion. I suppose that all the members of the House are aware of the atlas which was published and which covers all the provinces. The lady whose employment my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) has been criticising is a native of British Columbia, and has been lecturing in Great Britain last year and this year. She has strict instructions to give British Columbia the full benefit of her talents and knowledge.

I suppose the hon. minister is referring to Miss Agnes Deans Cameron. To what class of people would her lectures be addressed? I can understand it would be that class in Great Britain who are likelv to come out with money to invest in fruit lands. But I presume that she would not direct her attention in lecturing work so much to the labouring class.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) has the idea exactly. But, besides lecturing, Miss Cameron furnishes articles Mr. BURRELL.
to magazines and newspapers which would be more likely to reach the people he has in mind. Besides Miss Cameron, our arrangement with the Salvation Army is with a special view to their attention to that particular side of the work that my hon. friend has mentioned, always with due consideration, of course, to the other side of the question. Our records show that British Columbia has not suffered so badly in the general effort to secure increase of population. Our statement is that in 1900 and, 1901 the immigration to British Columbia of which we had knowledge was 2,600, and in 1909-10 the immigration of which we had knowledge was 30,721.

Of course my hon. friend would not wish to assume for a moment that' that was all due to the immigration work of the Dominion department. I do not wish to minimize the work of the Dominion, but the provincial government has gone to a great deal of expense of a special kind to promote immigration. I want to impress on the minister the strong need of immigration into British Columbia to meet the serious conditions that exist there now.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quite appreciate the situation and can assure my hon. friend that our department in Great Britain is cooperating with the British Columbia department in every way possible. Samples of British Columbia fruit are given display in our offices and in every way we are working in harmony with the British Columbia government. I do not wish to claim that this large movement was entirely the work of the Dominion, but I point out that the province has at least had some consideration in the flow of immigration.
Winnipeg and St. Boniface hospital, $15,000.
How is that divided? It does not seem a large sum.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Accounts are rendered and checked. This sum is to provide for the treatment of immigrants who have been less than one year in the country. The hospitals charge $1 per day for each immigrant treated, one-half being paid by the Dominion and one half by the provincial government. The expenditure in 1909-10 was for the St. Boniface hospital, 3,590 days at 50 cents per day, $1,795; and for the Winnipeg General hospital, 7,288 days at 50 cents a day, $3,644, a total of $5,439.

It seems hardly fair to make the province pay one half. Of course they pay all hospitals for all patients but it seems hardly fair to make them pay for the immigrants who have been in the province less than a year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course it is a matter of compromise.
Why is there no report of the Chief Medical Officer in the current report of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was in Germany at the time of the compilation of the report, and his report will appear separately.

The minister said that if a man had $25 it did not matter to the department where he got it, whether it was by charity or not. How does that work in the case of an immigrant helped by a charity society at home?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is quite a difference between the man who borrows $25 and the man who is given his passage or assistanc,-. out. If the charitable society pays the man's passage and furnishes him with $25 that he would have on his arrival here, we would not question his entry. The exclusion of the charity aided immigrant, was made to meet the case of the charitable society furnishing an immigrant with a passage to Canada, and landing him here without means of support or employment.
As long as they lend him the extra $25 you accept him?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If he is sound physically.
I suppose we have fairly definite information as to the mini ber of Americans who have come into Canada as settlers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the fiscal year 1909, 103,798; for the 10 months to the end of January, 1911, this fiscal year, 102,017 people who came from the United States to settle in Canada.
Have we as definite information as to how many people have gone from Canada to the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would add to the expense of administration and we did not realize that there would be the serious benefit that would warrant us in going to the expense.

Then how would we know what we were gaining? There might be half as many going to the United States as came into Canada. It would be hardly business to say that we were getting 104,090 or whatever the number was, in the year, if we have half as many going from Canada back again,	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is a matter of judgment whether we should go to the expense or not. No doubt we could get the information, but
it would cost something, and the material result would not be altered. If we have the people we have them, whether we count them or not.
And if they have gone back we have not got them.

I remember distinctly in the old days when the government used to keep a record of all that came in and no record of those that went out; and I also recollect when the census was taken the very comfortable position the government was in; they would not find their natural increase, and showed nothing but the immigrants that came in.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it would be a great mistake to assume that all the people who have come into the country have remained in it. I am not taking that position; I merely say that we have counted this many people coming in, and we have not taken account of the people who went out. Of course the census will tell the tale. I am afraid that those who have been building on all the people who have come into the country remaining here, will find themselves at sea.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of Mr. Graham, House adjourned at 11.28 p.m.

Tuesday, March 14, 1911.
